Angle

GeometryConstructions
Game: Move the two rays and watch the angle get its name: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex, full, or big.
How to play: Drag a blue dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Type a number of degrees, press + or −, or tick "Signed angle" to see which way the turn goes.
Look for the math

The same two rays can be named in several ways. What decides the name is not how far apart the dots look, but how far one ray has turned from the other.

Measure the turn

A whole turn is 360°, so a quarter turn is 90° and half a turn is 180°. The applet measures the turn in whole degrees and rounds the number before it gives the angle a name. That rounding is real: 89.6° rounds to 90° and is called right, while 89.4° is called acute.

Seven names for one picture

The old applet's own code checks the absolute value of the rounded number in this order: 0 → zero, 90 → right, less than 90 → acute, less than 180 → obtuse, 180 → straight, less than 360 → reflex, 360 → full, and anything bigger → big. A turn of 370° ends in the same place as one of 10°, yet the applet still calls it big because it remembers the turn you made.

Positive and negative turns

With Signed angle on, a turn one way is positive and a turn the other way is negative. The sign is printed after the name, but the name itself uses the size of the turn, so −30° and 30° are both acute. Turning ray OA moves both rays together and leaves the measured turn alone; turning ray OB changes it. The Java applet only let you drag OA and type the number — here OB can be dragged as well, and the turn is rounded to whole degrees just like the numbers you type.

Try the presets in order: 0°, 90°, 180°, 360°. Then use the + button to step just past a boundary and watch the name jump.
